inline.s: yi] bright and distinct in appearance; flickering in appearance.] [Five skandhas: also called the five aggregates, namely the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of thought, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; these are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Of these, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the ‘dharma of form’; the four aggregates of feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the ‘dharmas of mind.’ The aggregate of form is the body, while the other four aggregates (feeling, thought, formations, consciousness) are the mind. Master Yinguang says: “The five skandhas are form, feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness. Form is the body produced by the retribution of karma; feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness are the illusory, deluded mind that arises upon contact with objects. From this illusory body and mind, upon the six sense objects, one gives rise to confusion and creates karma.” (From the Essential Selections of Master Yinguang’s Writings.) The Nirvana Sutra says: “At the moment of death one’s relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot control himself; the good and evil of his whole life all appear before him at once. After the warmth [of the body] is exhausted, the past five skandhas cease and the present intermediate being is born. After entering the womb, the present intermediate being ceases and the future five skandhas are born. It is like light arising as darkness ceases, and darkness arising as light ceases, continuing without a break.”] [Six entries: the six faculties entering the six objects is called ‘six entries,’ namely: eye enters form, ear enters sound, nose enters smell, tongue enters taste, body enters touch, and mind enters dharmas. The six entries are also another name for the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind).] [Twelve places and eighteen realms: the six faculties plus the six objects together are called the twelve places. ‘Place’ holds the meaning of arising, for from the six faculties and six objects the six consciousnesses arise. Thus the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses together form the eighteen realms.] [Twenty-five existences: because fruits of existence are produced from karmic causes, the fruit is also called an ‘existence.’ The fruits of the three realms are divided into twenty-five categories, known as the twenty-five existences. Of these, the desire realm has fourteen existences, namely the four evil destinies (also called the four evil paths: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras), the four continents (Eastern Purvavideha, Southern Jambudvipa, Western Godaniya, and Northern Uttarakuru), and the six desire heavens. The form realm has seven existences, namely the four dhyana heavens as four existences, and, in addition, the Great Brahma heaven, the five Pure Abode heavens, and the No-thought heaven as three existences. The formless realm has four existences, namely the four stations of emptiness.]
Once this entire chain has been born
, then bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and Buddha-nature appear before one; and at the moment they appear there is also no measure to their appearing. Hence the ancient worthy
having realized this, could say: ‘When responding to the eye, it is like a thousand suns

, and the ten thousand forms cannot escape its shadow and substance; when responding to the ear, it is like a deep valley, and great and small sounds alike are all fully [heard].’ Such things do not depend on seeking from another, do not borrow another’s power, but arise of themselves, vividly alive, in the place where one responds to conditions.
If you have not yet attained this, then turn this mind that ponders the dusty toils of the world back to the place where pondering cannot reach. Try to ponder it and see:

one is the place that pondering cannot reach? A monk asked Zhaozhou: “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?” Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu’ (Not). Just this one word—whatever cleverness you have, please arrange it, please reckon it. When pondering, reckoning, and arranging leave no place to set them down, and you feel only a stifling in the belly and vexation in the heart, that is exactly the good season; the eighth consciousness is on the point of being brought to rest. When you feel it so, do not let go, but keep lifting and pulling on just this one word ‘Wu.’ Lift it and pull it again and again, and what was unfamiliar naturally becomes familiar, while what was familiar naturally becomes unfamiliar.

As long as emotional consciousness is not broken through, the heart-fire flickers on. At just such a moment, merely take up the topic of your doubt and keep hold of it. As when a monk asked Zhaozhou: “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?” Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ Just keep lifting it up and being aware of it. Coming from the left is not it, coming from the right is not it; nor may you seek to wait for enlightenment with the mind, nor claim it at the place where it is raised, nor take it as a mysterious comprehension, nor deliberate over it as existence or non-existence, nor conjecture it as the ‘no’ of a true nothing, nor sit within the shell of ‘nothing to do,’ nor grasp it at the place of striking fire from stone or a flash of lightning. When at last there is no mind to apply, and the mind has no place to rest, do not fear falling into emptiness—here is the good place. Suddenly, when a mouse enters a cow’s horn, you will see it broken off.

Continue only to lift and pull from time to time. When deluded thoughts arise, there is no need to check them with a stilling mind—just watch the huatou. Lifting while walking, lifting while sitting. Lift it and pull it, until it has no flavor; then is the good place, and one must not let go. Suddenly the flower of the mind blossoms and illumines the lands of the ten directions, and one can, upon the tip of a single hair, manifest the jewel-king lands, and, seated within a single particle of dust, turn the great Dharma-wheel.
